title: Radical plan on surgery waitlist
full_text:
Public to go private Ambitious plans to slash public elective surgery waiting lists by moving minor cases to private day hospitals will be outlined at a major conference in Adelaide next week.
The blueprint claims the plan is budget-neutral, would not mean longer waits for private patients – and may prove a saviour for the sector.
The Day Hospitals Australia (DHA) conference at Adelaide Convention Centre from Wednesday to Friday – which will include Health Minister Mark Butler and opposition health spokeswoman Anne Ruston – will be told more than 50 private day hospitals have shut nationally in the past five years.
These include four in South Australia – South Terrace Urology, West Lakes Day Surgery, Oxford Day Surgery Centre and Waverley House Plastic Surgery Centre – leaving 24 day clinics in the state.
DHA chief executive Jane Griffiths said reforms allowing patients on public waiting lists to have their surgery in day hospitals would be a cost-effective initiative, rather than the public sector outsourcing patients to larger private hospitals with overnight beds at greater expense.
“Day hospitals provide quality, safe, efficient and cost-effective care,” she said.
“We want to see public waitlist targets linked to private capacity. This would reduce public surgery waiting lists, improve patient outcomes through timely care and put downward pressure on private health insurance premiums.
“This will assist in reducing the waiting lists in SA and allow the public sector to accommodate more complex cases.
“The process of outsourcing in SA needs to be more streamlined and centralised.” Under the plan, a Private Efficient Price would ensure hospitals were paid equitably for the same procedures, which an independent report for DHA estimates could deliver up to $1bn in annual savings.
A new Type D category would be introduced in the private system, allowing selected same-day procedures to be performed in stand-alone day hospitals.
Starting with ophthalmology and diagnostic gastroenterology, the DHA’s consultant’s report estimates $200m in savings could be achieved each year, scaling up to 29 surgical treatments and $500m in annual savings.
The reform blueprint also notes: “This would place downward pressure on private health insurance premiums, providing hip-pocket relief for Australians seeking elective surgery.” Ms Griffiths stressed the proposal would not mean people with private health insurance would face longer queues, noting the 357 day hospitals across Australia treated about one million patients a year but still had plenty of excess capacity. As of Thursday, SA Health had 25,424 public patients listed as “ready for elective surgery” including 6831 listed as overdue. Ophthalmology had the most patients ready with 3931 including 888 overdue, while other specialties included urology with 3091 patients ready, including 1306 overdue.
